analysis.one_liner: Caps the amount anyone can give to super PACs, restoring contribution limits removed in 2010.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a single cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Rules Committee in May 2026 and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal election law so that committees that spend money independently in elections — commonly called super PACs — are subject to the same caps on contributions as other political committees. Those caps were removed for super PACs by a 2010 court decision. The bill's findings note that in 2024, super PACs spent heavily in elections and that nearly all individual super PAC money came from the very wealthiest donors. The bill was introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders with one cosponsor and referred to the Senate Rules Committee, where it has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who believe large donations buy political access. The bill would cap what any single donor can give to a super PAC, reducing the ability of a handful of billionaires to fund advertisements that dominate elections, and it would make it harder to route money through super PACs to influence candidates.

how_it_helps.text: It would apply the same contribution limits that already apply to other political committees to committees that make independent expenditures, ending the unlimited contributions super PACs currently accept.
The bill's stated purposes are to limit the risk of corrupt agreements between candidates and large contributors, limit the appearance of corruption, and restore public faith in elections.
By requiring contributions to pass through a regulated committee rather than flowing directly to a super PAC, it would make it harder for foreign money to reach U.S. elections through intermediaries.

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs and the donors who currently give them unlimited sums — in 2024, nearly all individual super PAC contributions came from the top 1% of donors. Political consultants and media firms that are paid from super PAC spending would also see less money flow their way.

drawbacks.text: The limits the bill would impose rest on authority a federal appeals court struck down in 2010 (SpeechNow.org v. FEC), so critics argue Congress cannot constitutionally cap super PAC contributions and that the bill would face an immediate legal challenge rather than take effect.

Restoring contribution limits would not, by itself, cap total campaign spending: wealthy donors could still fund other vehicles for political speech, so some critics argue the bill addresses a channel rather than the underlying flow of money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: contribution limits would shrink the channel through which a tiny group of megadonors funds federal elections, and the bill's findings document a measurable concentration of money in a few hands. The strongest objection is legal rather than practical — a federal appeals court barred these limits in 2010, so opponents argue Congress cannot enact them without a constitutional amendment or a change in that precedent — and the bill would not, by itself, address overall campaign spending. As written and with one cosponsor, it has had no practical effect.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Rules and Administration Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on May 20, 2026, and the Senate immediately referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history.
Only one senator, a Democrat, signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill's findings say independent spending rose more than 700% between 2008 and 2020, and that in 2024 the top 1% of individual super PAC donors provided 96.94% of individual super PAC contributions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Super PACs and the large donors who fund them, since the current unlimited-contribution system continues unchanged. Whether that changes will depend on whether the Rules Committee acts before the Congress ends.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap contributions to super PACs.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over election law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in May 2026 and has taken no action on the bill since.

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Have not brought campaign finance overhaul measures to the Senate floor, as is typical for measures of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: Only a Democratic cosponsor joined the independent sponsor, and no votes have occurred, so no party split can be measured.

industries.industry: Super PACs and their major donors
industries.note: The bill would subject super PACs to the same contribution caps as other committees, ending their ability to accept unlimited sums from single donors. Its findings report that the top 1% of individual donors provided nearly 97% of all individual super PAC contributions in 2024.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign media firms
industries.note: A large share of super PAC money pays for advertising and consulting; capping super PAC fundraising would shrink that revenue stream. This is an inference from the bill's mechanism rather than something the record states directly.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no committee action, and a 55-seat Republican majority in the Senate, the bill is very likely to die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027, as most campaign finance bills do. A court decision limiting Congress's power over campaign spending makes passage unlikely under any Congress.
